subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography — Glaciation (Consolidated Reading)
description: Consolidated reading passages for KS3 Glaciation, drawn from three source packs. Covers glacier formation, glacial erosion, depositional landforms (moraine, drumlins, erratics) and the management of tourism in glacial landscapes. Passages progress from introductory overviews to more detailed accounts.

data.sourcePassage: A glacier is a large moving body of ice that flows slowly because of gravity. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls than melts. This build-up of snow is called accumulation. As layer after layer of snow piles up, the lower snow is compressed by the weight above it and becomes dense firn. Over hundreds of years, firn turns into glacier ice. The heavy ice then starts to move downhill. In warmer periods, melting called ablation may happen at the snout. If melting is faster than forward movement, the glacier retreats.

questions.question: What is the term for the build-up of snow where more falls than melts?
questions.modelAnswer: Accumulation

questions.question: How does snow change into firn?
questions.modelAnswer: It is compressed by the weight of layers of snow above it until it becomes dense and compacted.

questions.question: Why does the glacier begin to move downhill?
questions.modelAnswer: The ice mass becomes very heavy, so gravity pulls it downhill.

questions.question: What does glacier retreat suggest about melting compared with forward movement?
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests that melting (ablation) is happening faster than the glacier is moving forward.

data.sourcePassage: Glaciers shape the land by weathering and erosion. Freeze-thaw weathering happens when water gets into cracks in rock, freezes, expands and breaks the rock apart. Two important erosional processes are plucking and abrasion. In plucking, meltwater freezes around rocks at the base or sides of the glacier, and the moving ice pulls them away. In abrasion, rock fragments carried by the glacier scrape and polish the rock beneath. These processes help create corries, steep back walls and wider, deeper valleys. Over time, a river valley can be widened and straightened into a U-shaped valley.

questions.question: Which two processes are named as the main types of glacial erosion?
questions.modelAnswer: Plucking and abrasion

questions.question: How is freeze-thaw different from plucking?
questions.modelAnswer: Freeze-thaw breaks rock apart in place, while plucking removes rock as glacier ice freezes around it and pulls it away.

questions.question: Why does abrasion help make valleys wider and deeper?
questions.modelAnswer: Because rocks carried by the glacier grind against the valley floor and sides, scraping away material.

questions.question: What evidence in a landscape might suggest past glaciation?
questions.modelAnswer: Features such as corries, steep back walls and U-shaped valleys suggest the landscape was shaped by glaciers in the past.

data.sourcePassage: When glacier ice melts, it drops the material it has been carrying. This deposited material is called moraine. Terminal moraine marks the furthest advance of the glacier, while lateral moraine is left along the sides. Medial moraine forms when two glaciers join and their side moraines combine. Drumlins are smooth hills shaped like half-buried eggs or teardrops. They point in the direction the glacier moved and often appear in groups called a drumlin field. Erratics are large rocks carried by the glacier and dropped far from their original source, sometimes on very different rock types.

questions.question: What is the name for material deposited by a glacier after melting?
questions.modelAnswer: Moraine

questions.question: How can terminal moraine help geographers understand the past glacier?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows the furthest point that the glacier reached before it retreated.

questions.question: Why do drumlins point in the direction of glacier movement?
questions.modelAnswer: Because the moving glacier streamlines the deposited material, tapering it in the direction of flow.

questions.question: Why might an erratic be a different rock type from the local area?
questions.modelAnswer: Because the glacier transported it from somewhere else and then dropped it after melting.

data.sourcePassage: When a glacier is moving, it carries rock fragments and sediment. If the glacier slows down or melts, it loses energy and drops this material. The deposited material is called moraine. Different patterns of moraine form in different places. Terminal moraine marks the glacier's furthest advance. Lateral moraine forms along the sides of the glacier. If two glaciers join, their side deposits can merge into a line of medial moraine. Ground moraine is spread across the valley floor after the ice has retreated.

questions.question: Why does a glacier drop the material it is carrying?
options: It loses energy when it slows or melts
The rock melts along with the ice
questions.modelAnswer: It loses energy when it slows or melts.

questions.question: Why might medial moraine only form in some valleys?
questions.modelAnswer: It only forms where two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join together.

questions.question: How is ground moraine different from terminal moraine in terms of where it is deposited?
questions.modelAnswer: Ground moraine is spread across the valley floor as the ice retreats, whereas terminal moraine forms a ridge at the glacier's furthest advance.

questions.question: Why is terminal moraine useful to geographers studying a glacier?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows how far the glacier advanced, helping geographers identify the former limit of the ice.

data.sourcePassage: Drumlins are depositional landforms made mainly of till. They are shaped like half-buried eggs or teardrops and are usually found in groups called drumlin fields. One explanation is that a glacier deposits material when it meets an obstruction or reaches a flatter valley floor. As the glacier keeps moving, the deposited material becomes streamlined into a smooth, tapered hill. Glaciers also leave erratics. These are large rocks carried away from their original source and dropped in an area with different rock types.

questions.question: What shape are drumlins usually described as?
questions.modelAnswer: They are usually shaped like teardrops or half-buried eggs.

questions.question: How does continued glacier movement help shape a drumlin?
questions.modelAnswer: As the glacier continues moving, it streamlines the deposited sediment into a smooth, tapered hill.

questions.question: What does the name 'drumlin field' tell you about where drumlins are found?
questions.modelAnswer: It tells you that many drumlins are found together in the same area.

questions.question: Why can erratics give clues about past glacier movement?
questions.modelAnswer: They show that rocks were transported from a different area by moving ice before being dropped when the glacier melted.

data.sourcePassage: Glacial landscapes attract many tourists because of their dramatic scenery and distinctive landforms, but they are also fragile environments. Places that attract large numbers of visitors are called honeypot sites. Tourism can create jobs and income, yet it can also damage vegetation, increase erosion on footpaths, disturb farm animals, and cause traffic congestion, noise and pollution. Overcrowding may also affect local people. Sustainable tourism means managing these competing pressures so the landscape can still be enjoyed in the future. Common responses include diverting walking routes, promoting public transport and cycling, keeping dogs on leads around farms, and using visitor centres to educate tourists.

questions.question: What is a honeypot site?
options: A place that attracts large numbers of tourists
A valley filled with glacier ice
A farm beside a mountain lake
questions.modelAnswer: A place that attracts large numbers of tourists.

questions.question: Give one environmental problem caused by tourism in glacial landscapes.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include vegetation being destroyed, footpath erosion, water or air pollution, or noise pollution.

questions.question: Why is sustainable tourism important in glacial landscapes?
questions.modelAnswer: Because these landscapes are fragile, so tourism must be managed carefully if future generations are to keep enjoying them.

questions.question: How do visitor centres and transport schemes help reduce conflict?
questions.modelAnswer: They educate visitors about responsible behaviour and reduce congestion by encouraging more sustainable travel choices.

data.sourcePassage: Different tourist activities can create different problems in glacial landscapes. Overused footpaths can destroy vegetation and erode the ground. Speedboats can create noise and water pollution. Dogs may disturb cattle on farmland, and heavy traffic can lead to congestion, air pollution and accidents. Managers try to reduce these conflicts in practical ways. They may divert popular routes to let land recover, set speed limits on lakes, keep dogs on leads around farms, promote public transport and bike paths, and educate visitors through visitor centres.

questions.question: Why might keeping dogs on leads help farmers in glacial areas?
questions.modelAnswer: It reduces the chance that dogs will disturb or chase cattle and livestock on farmland.

questions.question: Why do managers divert popular walking routes rather than simply closing them?
questions.modelAnswer: Diverting routes allows the damaged land time to recover while still letting people enjoy the landscape.

questions.question: Which management method in the passage is most focused on changing visitor behaviour rather than controlling vehicles or routes? Explain your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Educating visitors through visitor centres is most focused on changing behaviour, because it aims to inform people rather than physically restrict what they can do.
